extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, judges, government engineers, and practitioners advising or litigating about navigable waters, riparian rights, and federal navigation/harbor regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal standards and principles governing what constitutes navigable waters of the United States, federal powers to regulate and remove obstructions, rights in submerged lands, and limits on state and private actions affecting navigation. Useful for legal analysis, permitting, and government project planning concerning navigation and harbor works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to regulate navigation (commerce clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has power under the commerce clause to legislate for the prevention and removal of physical obstructions to navigation and to regulate navigation over navigable waters of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical statutes (acts of 1884, 1888, 1890, 1899, 1906, etc.) progressively vested duties and powers (often through the Secretary of War/Chief of Engineers) to require removal/alteration of obstructions, establish harbor lines, forbid certain deposits/works, and enforce compliance (including penalties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'navigable in fact' / navigable waters of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: A river is a navigable water of the United States when it is navigable in fact: used or susceptible of being used in its ordinary condition as a highway for commerce with other States or foreign countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capability of use by the public for transportation/commerce (regardless of vessel type or difficulty) is the controlling test. Citations and examples: Daniel Ball, Montello, and case law showing state statutes declaring small streams navigable do not make them navigable under U.S. law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: federal vs state navigable waters
rubrics_metrics.description: Waters navigable only for commerce within a state (not forming a highway for interstate or foreign commerce) are navigable waters of the State, not of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the stream does not form (by itself or by connection) a continued highway for interstate or foreign commerce, federal navigation statutes/controls do not apply—examples include Devil's Lake (ND) and other wholly intrastate waters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity/connection requirement for federal navigability
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a U.S. navigable water, the waterway must form, by itself or by uniting with other waters, a continued highway over which commerce is or may be carried on with other States or foreign countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermittent navigable stretches separated by non-navigable segments (e.g., French Broad River with separated navigable stretches) do not make the entire stream a U.S. navigable water unless there is continuity of navigation or navigable capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War (Chief of Engineers) authority over bridges and obstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes authorize the Secretary of War to require owners/operators of bridges (and other structures) that obstruct navigation to provide aids or alter/remove structures to render navigation free, easy, and unobstructed; failure to comply can trigger penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts required submission and approval of bridge locations/plans; statutes provided notice-and-hearing protections and specific penalties (e.g., monthly fines) and enforcement mechanisms via the Department of Justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on erecting structures or filling without permission
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unlawful to erect wharves, dams, breakwaters, or to excavate/fill in navigable waters of the United States without permission of the Secretary of War (or other designated federal authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory prohibition aims to prevent obstructions; related sections also forbid depositing refuse matter where it would obstruct navigation and allow establishment of harbor lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of wrecks and enforcement of removal of obstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal statutes authorize removal of wrecks and provide enforcement for removal of obstructions to navigation, including penalties and Department of Justice enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections of the river-and-harbor legislation (e.g., sections 9–20 of the 1899 act) allocate responsibilities and penalties; Secretary of War and Justice Department roles are described in opinions and historic statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition extends beyond physical structures to changes impairing navigable capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes forbid not only physical obstructions but any changes (wherever done or however done) that tend to destroy the navigable capacity of a navigable water of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court interpretations (e.g., U.S. v. Rio Grande Irrigation Co.) treat 'obstruction' as including anything that impairs navigable capacity; 'channel' may be construed broadly to include entire river bed and flowing water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal/diversion of water that impairs navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawal of water (e.g., for irrigation by pumps) that seriously impairs a river's navigable capacity is within federal prohibition and may be limited or prevented by federal authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The War Department has recommended limiting or prohibiting further diversion where navigable capacity is affected; the statute applies to such diversions even if they do not involve constructing a structure in the stream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of floatable streams and Congress's competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether 'floatable' streams (usable only for floating logs/timber) are included in the term 'navigable waters of the United States' can be doubtful, but Congress may, under the commerce clause, control such streams when treated as highways of interstate commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions note doubt but recognize congressional authority to regulate these streams as interstate highways if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private ownership of submerged land subject to public navigation servitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Title to beds and shores of navigable waters is generally in the State or riparian owners, but such title is subject to a public servitude/easement for navigation and to the United States' power to regulate navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners cannot lawfully fill or otherwise deprive the public of navigable use; grants of submerged land are qualified by an implied reservation that allows improvements in aid of navigation without compensation in many circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States' authority to use/occupy submerged land for navigation improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States may occupy or use submerged lands for purposes in aid of navigation and may dredge, maintain wharves, and take other actions necessary to improve navigation, often without compensation to state grantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While title remains with State or grantee, the land is subject to the federal servitude; government may exercise powers to dredge, lay conduits, build piers in aid of navigation or defense, and the State's statutes cannot constrain such federal operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of federal improvement on private tolls and franchises
rubrics_metrics.description: A private company that aided or cooperated in federal improvement and then levied tolls on navigation could be found to be creating an unlawful obstruction; conversely, corporations that improved navigation under valid state contracts may have legitimate franchises and toll rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show a distinction: improvements under public authorization or state contract (e.g., Carondolet Canal & Navigation Co.) can yield enforceable toll rights, whereas imposing tolls on publicly improved channels may be unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures built without congressional authority subject to alteration without compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures placed under navigable waters without authority of Congress are presumptively subject to modification or removal in the interest of navigation without compensation to the builders/owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional resolutions or orders can require alteration of unauthorized structures (e.g., tunnels under Chicago River) because owners are presumed to have known the regulatory risk when building without federal authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal projects do not necessarily vest soil title in United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of government works (dykes, piers, etc.) under appropriations for navigation does not of itself vest title to the soil in the United States; the U.S. interest is limited to the navigational/use purpose and conservation of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners retain property rights and may use their land so long as such use does not obstruct navigation or interfere with the federal improvement; federal exercise may be discontinued or abandoned when no longer needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leases and private rights over submerged lands are qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: Leases or grants of submerged lands (e.g., oyster leases) are qualified by the public right of navigation and subject to interruption or interference by federal navigation improvements without necessarily extinguishing leaseholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal improvement projects need not extinguish private leasehold interests for navigation purposes; lessees run the risk that crops or uses may be interfered with by navigation improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel/prescriptive acquisition and prior federal reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the United States has reserved land (e.g., military reservations) prior to state grants, the U.S. may have title or prescriptive rights (e.g., for wharves) that limit subsequent grantees' use of submerged lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reservations declared before state grants can create servitudes in favor of the United States for defensive or navigational purposes; government use may be characterized as acquisitive by prescription in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: State police powers coexist but are limited by federal navigation authority
rubrics_metrics.description: State control over internal matters (fisheries, sanitary uses, shores, etc.) remains except where matters concern interstate/foreign commerce or structures that obstruct navigation and thus require federal authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sewer outlets—states may regulate sanitation but cannot override federal authority over structures obstructing navigation; federal permission (Chief of Engineers/Secretary) is needed for obstructive works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbor lines and overlapping federal statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment of harbor lines under later statutes does not necessarily oust earlier, more specific federal jurisdiction (e.g., earlier dumping prohibitions in New York basins remain in force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes and administrative actions must be read in context; specific earlier federal prohibitions can coexist with later harbor line designations and other federal regulations.
